`0.028` seconds in my validation runs.  ### Impact  This is an availability issue in Pillow's PDF append handling. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route.  The demonstrated primitive is deterministic CPU/resource amplification from compact attacker-controlled PDF bytes. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`.  Requires attacker-influenced existing PDF processed by Pillow's documented PDF append path; not ordinary Image.open().  This should not be treated as just an unexpected Python exception. In the tested affected builds, the malformed PDF is accepted and processed to normal completion after the expensive expansion.  ### Remediation  Reject duplicate and cyclic page-tree references before constructing `self.pages` and `self.orig_pages`.  One possible fix is to pass traversal state through `linearize_page_tree()`:  - Track active `/Pages` references to reject cycles. - Track seen page-tree and page indirect references to reject duplicate references. - Raise `PdfFormatError` when the page tree is not an acyclic tree of unique indirect references.  Suggested regression tests:  - A small PDF whose `/Kids` array repeats the same child `/Pages` reference should raise `PdfFormatError` quickly when used through `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`. - A normal nested linear page tree should continue to append successfully.

``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.  In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.  The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says `SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB` is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF `ImageWidth=2**27` kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The `tiffinfo=` route dates back to Pillow 2.3.0 (`dbf47837ce99`), and the `exif=` route to 8.4.0 (`c0f619384cbc`).  ## Details  When an image is saved as TIFF through the libtiff encoder (any `compression=` other than raw, or `TiffImagePlugin.WRITE_LIBTIFF`), libtiff sizes its scanline from the `ImageWidth` / `SamplesPerPixel` / `BitsPerSample` / `PlanarConfiguration` tags it was handed, Pillow sizes the encoder row buffer from the real image, and nothing compares the two. In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch only `BitsPerSample` is pinned in the attribute dict given to the encoder (`atts`, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955-1982`); the other geometry tags can come from caller- or attacker-supplied data:  - `ImageWidth` (256), `ImageLength` (257) and `PlanarConfiguration` (284) are set from `im.size` *before* the `tiffinfo=` / `exif=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`, so they are overwritten by it — by the EXIF of an uploaded JPEG, or by stale geometry in `im.getexif()` / `im.tag_v2` of a TIFF that Pillow auto-transposed on load (Orientation tag) or that the application `thumbnail()`ed. - `SamplesPerPixel` (277) is only put in the IFD for multi-band modes (`:1847-1850`), so for single-band images (`L`, `P`, `I;16`, `1`, …) a value from `exif=` / `tiffinfo=`, or from the *source TIFF's own IFD* via `supplied_tags` (`im.tag_v2`, `:1782`), is forwarded to libtiff. A palette TIFF with `SamplesPerPixel=2, BitsPerSample=(8,8), ExtraSamples=(0,)` opens as mode `P` (rawmode `PX`, extra sample dropped), and a bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` — no save arguments; `compression` and `Predictor` are inherited from the source — already makes libtiff process `2*width` bytes per row from a `width`-byte buffer.  `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then hands the image-sized row buffer to `TIFFWriteScanline`, and libtiff reads one scanline of the *tag-described* geometry out of a buffer holding one row of the *actual* image. With `Predictor = 2` (also forwarded from `tiffinfo=` / `im.tag_v2`) libtiff's horizontal differencing first rewrites the whole scanline **in place**, so the over-read becomes an out-of-bounds heap **write** on every row.  The tags do not have to be supplied deliberately by the application: `im.getexif()` of an uploaded JPEG returns whatever IFD0 tags the file carries, and the common metadata-preserving conversion  ```python im = Image.open(uploaded_jpeg)                                   # 64x4, mode "L" im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw") ```  behaves as follows on the stock build at this commit:  - EXIF IFD0 `{277: 3, 262: 2}` (SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB): the save succeeds and `out` is a 64x4 **RGB** TIFF. Re-opening it, the first 64 bytes of every 192-byte row are the image (0x11 fill); the remaining 128 bytes are heap that followed the 64-byte row buffer — e.g. `... 807a97e6527f0000 ... f03632e5527f0000 40832ee5527f0000` (x86-64 heap pointers), different on every run. - EXIF IFD0 `{256: 1<<27}` (ImageWidth=2^27): the process dies with SIGSEGV; gdb shows `TIFFWriteScanline (libtiff.so.6) ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. - valgrind on the first case: `Invalid read of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 64 alloc'd at calloc by _setimage`. - Control: the same JPEG with an EXIF holding only `Software` produces a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 pixel bytes are all 0x11.  The write variant needs nothing more than a well-formed 222-byte TIFF and the `exif=im.getexif()` idiom the project's own tests use (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_exif`, `test_modify_exif`); the interpreter dies with glibc's `free(): invalid next size (fast)` (SIGABRT):  ```python from PIL import Image; import io b = io.BytesIO() Image.new("RGB", (64, 4)).save(b, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={274: 6, 317: 2})  # Orientation=6, Predictor=2 im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(b.getvalue())); im.load()   # auto-transposed to 4x64; tag_v2/getexif() still say 64x4 im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF", exif=im.getexif())       # or tiffinfo=im.tag_v2 ```  Here libtiff processes 192-byte rows (64 px × 3 samples) from the 12-byte buffer `_setimage` allocated for a 4-pixel RGB row, and `PredictorEncodeRow` rewrites the 180 heap bytes that follow it on each of 64 rows; valgrind on a `-g` build reports `Invalid write of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode (TiffDecode.c:1035) … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 12 alloc'd … by _setimage (encode.c:293)`. `im.thumbnail((8, 8))` before the save instead of the Orientation tag reaches the same state, as does the purely programmatic `Image.new("RGB", (128, 32)).save(fp, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={256: 1024, 257: 128, 317: 2})` (SIGSEGV). For the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route, a crafted <2 KB palette `PX` TIFF with `Compression = LZW, Predictor = 2` kills the stock build on a bare `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`; with a predictor-less codec the same re-save returns normally with `width` bytes of heap per row encoded into the output.  ### Walk-through  `_save` seeds the output IFD from the image and then copies the caller's tags over it:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py 1746    libtiff = WRITE_LIBTIFF or compression != "raw" 1749    ifd[PLANAR_CONFIGURATION] = 1 1751    ifd[IMAGEWIDTH] = im.size[0] 1752    ifd[IMAGELENGTH] = im.size[1]         … 1757    elif "exif" in encoderinfo: 1758        info = encoderinfo["exif"]          # Image.Exif, or bytes → Exif         … 1768    for key in info:             … 1772            ifd[key] = info.get(key)            # 256/257/277/262/284/317 … overwrite the above ```  The geometry is only partially re-asserted afterwards: `BITSPERSAMPLE` is always set, but `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` only for multi-band modes and `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` never:  ```python 1847    if bits != (1,): 1848        ifd[BITSPERSAMPLE] = bits 1849        if len(bits) != 1: 1850            ifd[SAMPLESPERPIXEL] = len(bits)    # not reached for L, P, I, F, I;16 … 1856    if PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION not in ifd:   # supplied value kept ```  In the libtiff branch every IFD entry that is not block-listed — and, after the IFD, every entry of `supplied_tags` (the source file's `im.tag_v2`) not already present — becomes a `TIFFSetField` argument. The only tag pinned to the image's real value is `BITSPERSAMPLE`:  ```python 1955        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]} 1959        for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):             … 1976            if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:                     …   atts[tag] = value 2002        encoder = Image._getencoder(im.mode, "libtiff", a, encoderconfig) 2003        encoder.setimage(im.im, (0, 0, *im.size)) ```  For the SamplesPerPixel=3 example the tag list passed to the encoder is `[(256, 64), (257, 4), (258, 8), (259, 5), (262, 2), (277, 3), (278, 4), (284, 1)]`; for the ImageWidth example it is `[(256, 134217728), (257, 4), (258, 8), …]`. 256 and 277 are in `core_tags` (`src/encode.c:694`), so `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` forwards them straight to `TIFFSetField`. For a single-band image `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` is absent from `ifd`, so the loop takes tag 277 from `supplied_tags` — the source TIFF's IFD — when one is present; the `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION == 2` adjustment at `:1783-1788` already compensates for this for separate-planes sources, the contiguous `PX` layout is the remaining case.  `encoder.setimage` sizes the packer's row buffer from the real image — 64 bytes for a 64-pixel `L` row:  ```c /* src/encode.c, _setimage */ 287    if (state->bits > 0) { 291        state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8; 293        state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes); ```  and `ImagingLibTiffEncode` packs one image row into it and gives the pointer to libtiff with no length:  ```c /* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c */ 1027        while (state->y < state->ysize) { 1028            state->shuffle(state->buffer, (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff] + …, state->xsize); 1035            if (TIFFWriteScanline(tiff, (tdata_t)(state->buffer), (uint32_t)state->y, 0) == -1) { ```  `TIFFWriteScanline` consumes `TIFFScanlineSize()` bytes, i.e. `ImageWidth * SamplesPerPixel * BitsPerSample / 8` as set through the tags. Nothing between `_save` and line 1035 compares that with `state->bytes`. With SamplesPerPixel=3 libtiff reads 192 bytes from the 64-byte block and LZW-encodes the trailing 128 heap bytes into the strip; with ImageWidth=2^27 it reads 128 MiB starting at the 64-byte block and faults. With `Predictor = 2`, libtiff's `PredictorEncodeRow` first runs horizontal differencing in place over the whole scanline (`bp[i] -= bp[i-stride]`), i.e. it rewrites the heap bytes that follow the block before encoding them; libtiff grows `ImageLength` as rows beyond the declared count are written, so every row of the real image goes through. A `PlanarConfiguration = 2` carried over from a planar source reaches libtiff by the same route; there libtiff's scanline (one sample plane) is shorter than Pillow's row, so the result is an undecodable file rather than an out-of-bounds access.  The non-libtiff path (`compression` absent/raw) is not affected: it goes through `ImagingRawEncode`, which treats the IFD-derived stride as padding and either zero-fills or fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG` (`src/libImaging/RawEncode.c:34-37,57-59`). Overriding `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` through `tiffinfo` on that path is an intended feature (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_tiff_chunks`).  The `exif=` route was introduced in `c0f619384cbc` ("Added "exif" keyword argument to save Image.Exif instance", 2021-07-04), first released in 8.4.0. The same override through `tiffinfo=` is older: it dates back to `dbf47837ce99` ("Add arbitrary tags to tiff images using an ImageFileDirectory", 2013-10-02, first in 2.3.0). The stale-geometry-from-the-file-itself form dates from `1b70a4c6b515` ("Use TIFF orientation", 2019-09-13, first in 6.2.0), which added the transpose on load.  ## Impact  Affected are applications that write TIFF output from user-supplied images through libtiff. Through the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route nothing more is needed than `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")` (format normalisation) on a crafted palette TIFF: `Compression`, `SamplesPerPixel` and `Predictor` are all inherited from the upload, so the uploader chooses between heap corruption / worker abort (`Predictor = 2`) and a normally-returning save whose output carries `width` bytes of the worker's heap per row. The `exif=` / `tiffinfo=` routes cover applications that convert to compressed TIFF while carrying the metadata across — `im.save(..., "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw"|"tiff_adobe_deflate"|"packbits"|"jpeg"|…, exif=im.getexif())`, `exif=im.info["exif"]`, or `tiffinfo=` built from the source file's tags. Neither option is a default, but both are ordinary settings for archival/print/scan pipelines and the idiom used in Pillow's own tests. The uploader then chooses the outcome through a few EXIF shorts: a small `SamplesPerPixel` (with a matching `Photometric` so the result is a valid RGB/CMYK TIFF) returns `(spp-1) × width` bytes of process heap per image row inside the produced file — for a 4000-pixel-wide upload that is 8 KB of heap per row, megabytes per file, readable with any TIFF decoder and containing allocator metadata, pointers (ASLR defeat) and whatever other requests left in freed memory; a large `ImageWidth` kills the worker with SIGSEGV; `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` larger than the (transposed or thumbnailed) image together with `Predictor = 2` writes `(declared_width − real_width) × bytes_per_pixel` bytes past a small fresh `calloc` block on every row — the values written are byte-wise differences of the existing heap contents, so the attacker controls extent and repetition but not directly the data; the observed result is heap corruption and abort of the whole worker, exploitation beyond that is not demonstrated. Because `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are routinely present in IFD0 of camera and scanner output, a benign photo that is resized before such a save also over-reads (its EXIF still describes the original width), so the crash variant can occur without an attacker.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow and only its public API; no rebuild is needed. It runs in well under a second.  It builds the attacker's input in memory: a 64x4 JPEG in mode `L` with every pixel set to 0x11, plus a chosen set of EXIF IFD0 tags. It then runs the metadata-preserving conversion an application would do:  ```python im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(jpeg)) im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw") ```  Finally it re-opens the TIFF that comes out. There are three cases:  - **control**: the EXIF holds only `Software`. The output is a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 bytes are all 0x11. The verdict can only be `BUG` if this holds. - **leak**: the EXIF holds `SamplesPerPixel=3, PhotometricInterpretation=RGB`. libtiff now treats each scanline as 192 bytes, but the row buffer only holds 64 bytes. The save still succeeds and the output is a 64x4 **`RGB`** TIFF. In each 192-byte row, the first 64 bytes are the image (0x11). The other 128 bytes are whatever sat in the heap after the 64-byte row buffer.   - The script hex-dumps row 0's extra bytes. They include x86-64 pointers such as `…e06c297e677f0000`, which change from run to run because of ASLR.   - It also counts the extra bytes that are neither 0x11 nor 0x00, since those could not have come from the image or from zero padding. On the stock build this is a few hundred of the 512 bytes (200–310 in our runs). - **crash**: the EXIF holds `ImageWidth=2**27`. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro crash`) with core dumps disabled. libtiff tries to read 128 MiB out of the 64-byte buffer, and the child dies with SIGSEGV (exit code -11).  Expected output on the stock build (the heap bytes and the count vary):  ``` control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True leak:    RGB (64, 4)          first 64 bytes of each row are the image (0x11): True          row 0, bytes 64..192 (past the row buffer):            0000000000000000310000000000000090e5b50669550000e06c297e677f0000            0000000001007900007b8804d80c0d8830000000000000001007000000000000            0100000000000000801a897e677f0000240300000000000030444a7d677f0000            4095487d677f0000885f897e677f000003000001010000000000000000000000          220 of 512 bytes past the row buffers are neither 0x11 nor 0x00 crash:   child exit code -11 (SIGSEGV) BUG ```  The last line is `BUG` if the control is clean and the leak case produced foreign bytes, the crash case died with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS, or both. Otherwise it is `OK`.  With either attached patch applied and rebuilt, the script prints:  ``` control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True leak:    output is not a readable image (no over-read) crash:   child exit code 0 (no signal) OK ```  In the leak case, the fixed build writes the image's real single sample per pixel but keeps the supplied `Photometric=RGB`. Pillow will not open a TIFF like that.  The out-of-bounds write variant is the three-line `Orientation=6, Predictor=2` snippet in Details (SIGABRT, `free(): invalid next size (fast)` on the stock build); for a file:line stack run it under valgrind on a `-g` build of the extensions.  ## Suggested fix  Two alternative patches are attached. Patch 2 is the Python-only subset of patch 1; patch 1 also hardens the C encoder.  **Attached patch 1** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`) does two independent things:  1. `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955` — the libtiff branch already pre-seeds `atts` with `BITSPERSAMPLE` so that no supplied tag can replace it. The patch extends that to the other tags that determine libtiff's scanline size, taken from the image being saved:  ```diff -        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]} +        atts: dict[int, Any] = { +            BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0], +            SAMPLESPERPIXEL: len(bits), +            IMAGEWIDTH: im.size[0], +            IMAGELENGTH: im.size[1], +            PLANAR_CONFIGURATION: 1, +        } ```     Doing it here rather than in the IFD built at 1749–1772 leaves the raw-writer behaviour exercised by `test_tiff_chunks` untouched, and because the merge loop visits `ifd` and `supplied_tags` only for tags not already in `atts`, it closes the `exif=`, `tiffinfo=` and source-IFD (`im.tag_v2`) routes alike. A supplied `PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION` still reaches the file (so EXIF `{277:3, 262:2}` now yields a 1-sample "RGB" TIFF that Pillow refuses to open); whether to force it to the mode's value is a format decision that no longer affects memory safety. For the re-saved `PX` palette case it may also be worth dropping the source's `EXTRASAMPLES` from `supplied_tags` (meaningless once the extra channel was discarded on load), as is already done for the planar case at `:1783-1788`, so the output is a self-consistent 1-sample palette file.  2. `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, `ImagingLibTiffEncode` — before the scanline loop, it refuses any configuration in which libtiff would read more than the packer produced, so the encoder stays safe regardless of where tags come from:  ```c         if (TIFFScanlineSize64(tiff) > (uint64_t)state->bytes) {             state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG;             ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup(state);             clientstate->tiff = NULL;             if (!clientstate->fp) {                 free(clientstate->data);             }             return -1;         } ```     The same cleanup is applied to the existing `TIFFWriteScanline` error path. For in-memory output, that path currently frees `clientstate->data` but leaves `clientstate->tiff` set, so the later `ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup` → `TIFFClose` → `TIFFFlush` writes into the freed buffer. Both error paths now close the TIFF before the data is freed. The `TIFFFlush` failure branch further down (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056`) has the same pattern and is left as it is.  **Attached patch 2** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` only) is step 1 above without the C changes, for maintainers who prefer not to touch the encoder. It closes every public-API route (`exif=`, `tiffinfo=`, a resized or transposed image's carried-over EXIF/`tag_v2`) by which these tags reach `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` still trusts its tag list, though, and the error-path use-after-free described above stays as it is.  Both patches add `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py::test_geometry_tags`, parametrised over oversized `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH`, `SAMPLESPERPIXEL=3` and `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION=2`. With either patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, `repro` prints `OK`, the `Predictor = 2` snippet in Details saves a 4×64 image normally, and the existing TIFF test suites still pass.  ## ``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-D7STJUWL [medium] CWE-770 dos Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927 in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes `Image.open()` return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service. The bug is in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` in `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new `bytes` object with `ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size)` and keeps it in `_tagdata`. `_safe_read()` only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling. The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF: * A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, via `_read_dpi_from_exif()`. * A 96 KB PNG `eXIf` chunk costs 754 MiB on `getexif()` or `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`. * WebP EXIF and MPO reach the same code. The attached reproducer builds a 72 KB TIFF and a 72 KB PNG. Using only `Image.open()` and `getexif()`, each causes 412 MiB of tag data to be retained, about 6,000 times the file size. The loop dates to the original PIL 1.1.7 import, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected. ## Details `TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` reads the out-of-line value of every IFD entry into its own `bytes` object and keeps it in `self._tagdata`. Nothing bounds the sum of those reads, and nothing prevents every entry from pointing at the same region of the file. An IFD with N entries whose `(offset, count)` each cover the whole file therefore costs N × filesize bytes of memory, while the IFD itself costs only 12 bytes per entry. This one loop is the IFD parser for TIFF frames and for `Image.Exif` alike, so it is reachable from `Image.open()` on a TIFF or JPEG and from `getexif()` / `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` on PNG, JPEG, WebP and MPO. Observed on the stock build at this commit: a valid 144,110-byte 1×1 greyscale TIFF with 12,000 such entries makes `Image.open()` return normally (no exception, no warning, 1 declared pixel so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is irrelevant) after 1.5 s, with the process RSS grown from 15 MiB to 1,671 MiB and `im.tag_v2` holding 1,649 MiB of tag data for as long as the image object lives. The same IFD placed in the `eXIf` chunk of a 96 KB PNG makes `im.getexif()` retain 754 MiB. A 65,870-byte JPEG whose APP1 `Exif` segment is such an IFD (5,400 entries × 65,519 bytes) allocates ~340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, with no further call. ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:902-946 (ImageFileDirectory_v2.load) for i in range(tag_count): tag, typ, count, data = ( … self._unpack("HHL4s", self._ensure_read(fp, 12))) … size = count * unit_size # 918: attacker-chosen if size > (8 if self._bigtiff else 4): here = fp.tell() (offset,) = self._unpack("Q" if self._bigtiff else "L", data) … fp.seek(offset) # 926: attacker-chosen data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size) # 927: new bytes object of `size` fp.seek(here) … self._tagdata[tag] = data # 945: kept self.tagtype[tag] = typ ``` `ImageFile._safe_read()` only guarantees that `size` bytes are actually present in the stream (it reads in `SAFEBLOCK` chunks and raises on truncation); it is a guard against allocating for data that does not exist, not against reading the same existing data many times. For a well-formed file each entry points at its own disjoint value, so the total read is at most the file size. For the crafted file every one of the N entries has a distinct tag number (so none overwrites another in `_tagdata`), type BYTE, `count = filesize - 1` and `offset = 1`; each iteration allocates and fills a fresh `filesize - 1`-byte object and stores it. `load()` does not care whether the tag number is known or whether the type makes sense for it; any 16-bit tag number and any type in `_load_dispatch` is accepted. Memory is `N × filesize`, and since `filesize ≈ 12 N`, it is quadratic in the file size: 12,000 entries / 144 KB → 1.6 GiB (measured); the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries / 786 KB → ~48 GiB; BigTIFF (`tag_count` is a `Q`) has no 16-bit entry limit at all. Reachability: - TIFF: `TiffImageFile._open()` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1187`) → `self._seek(0)` (`:1210`) → `self.tag_v2.load(self.fp)` (`:1258`, and again at `:1271`). This runs inside `Image.open()`, before `load()` and before any size check (`_decompression_bomb_check` only looks at `width × height` and is satisfied by the 1×1 image), and the resulting directory stays referenced as `im.tag_v2`. `_seek()` parses the IFD twice, but `reset()` drops the first copy, so the peak does not double; it is paid again for every frame on `seek()`/`n_frames`. - EXIF in other formats: `Image.Exif.load()` / `load_from_fp()` / `_get_ifd_dict()` (`Image.py:4146-4196`, `:4119-4133`) wrap the same `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` around the EXIF blob. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_eXIf` (`PngImagePlugin.py:697`) stores the whole chunk as `info["exif"]`, `JpegImagePlugin` concatenates APP1 `Exif` segments into `info["exif"]` (`JpegImagePlugin.py:114-117`), and WebP exposes its EXIF chunk the same way; `im.getexif()`, `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` and `_getexif()` then parse it and keep the values in `im._exif`. For JPEG no explicit call is needed: `JpegImageFile._open()` ends with `self._read_dpi_from_exif()` (`JpegImagePlugin.py:413`), which calls `getexif()` whenever no JFIF DPI is present, so the APP1 IFD is parsed during `Image.open()`. Note that an EXIF blob is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop via `_get_ifd_dict`), each through its own `load()` call. The only failure path in `load()` is `except OSError` → warning; running out of memory is not an `OSError`, so on Linux the realistic outcome for a larger N is the kernel OOM killer terminating the process rather than a Python exception. The loop predates Pillow: it came in with the PIL 1.1.7 import in `9a640e315715` ("Forking PIL", 2010-07-30) and was carried over unchanged into `ImageFileDirectory_v2`, so every release since 1.0 is affected. The per-tag `_safe_read` bounding added in the CVE-2019-16865 era does not address the sum. ## Impact Any service that calls `Image.open()` on an uploaded TIFF or JPEG — or `getexif()` / `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` on an uploaded PNG, JPEG or WebP, which thumbnailers routinely do to honour orientation — can be made to allocate and retain memory roughly `entries × filesize`, i.e. thousands of times the upload size, from a file of a few hundred KB that declares a 1×1 image and passes the decompression-bomb check. A ~800 KB TIFF requests ~48 GiB; in practice the worker (or its container) is OOM-killed within seconds, taking down all requests it was serving, and repeated uploads keep it down. No pixel decoding, `load()`, or further API call is required for the TIFF and JPEG cases, `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not apply, and no `DecompressionBomb*` warning gives the application a chance to refuse the file. There is no memory corruption; the effect is denial of service of the process handling the input. This is the same class as CVE-2021-27921/27922/27923 (BLP/ICNS/ICO "arbitrarily large memory allocations" from unchecked reported sizes, fixed in 8.1.2) and CVE-2021-28675 (PSD layer count not checked against the data size, DoS on `Image.open()` prior to `load()`), here in the TIFF/EXIF directory parser shared by several formats. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the stock Pillow in `/src`; nothing is compiled. It needs about 1 GB of free RAM (it caps its own address space at 4 GiB so that a larger run ends in `MemoryError` rather than the OOM killer). **Input.** `aliased_ifd()` builds, in memory, a little-endian classic TIFF: an 8-byte header, one IFD, nothing else. Every crafted entry is a private tag (1000 upwards) of type BYTE with `offset = 1` and `count = file size - 1`, i.e. each claims the whole file body as its value. Each costs 12 bytes in the file but a full file-sized read in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()`. **TIFF path.** The first file adds 8 ordinary tags (ImageWidth = ImageLength = 1, BitsPerSample = 8, no compression, BlackIsZero, one 1-byte strip pointing at a header byte) so that Pillow accepts it as a 1×1 `L` image, plus 6,000 aliased tags (72,110 bytes). Because the image is 1×1, `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` never comes into play. The script calls `Image.open()` on it and nothing else: no `load()`, no pixel access. **EXIF path.** The same 6,000-entry IFD (without the image tags) is passed as `exif=` when saving a 1×1 PNG, so it lands in an `eXIf` chunk; the script opens that PNG and calls `im.getexif()`, which is what `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` calls. **Check.** For each path the script reads `VmRSS` from `/proc/self/status` before and after, and adds up `len()` over the resulting directory's `_tagdata`. In a well-formed IFD each entry points at its own bytes, so the tag data can never be larger than the file. The script prints `BUG` if both the TIFF's `im.tag_v2` and the PNG's EXIF directory hold more than 2000× the size of their file, otherwise `OK`. On this commit each holds 412 MiB (~6000× the file) and RSS grows by about as much for each. The memory cost is entries × file size, and the file size itself grows at 12 bytes per entry, so the cost is quadratic: doubling to 12,000 entries (144 KB) gives the 1.6 GiB quoted above, and the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries (~786 KB file) comes to ~48 GiB. A JPEG APP1 segment or a WebP EXIF chunk carrying the same IFD behaves like the PNG case (for JPEG, already during `Image.open()`). ## Suggested fix The attached patch bounds the out-of-line tag data a single `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` call may pull in by the length of the stream it reads from. The values of a well-formed IFD do not overlap, so their total can never exceed the file; only aliased entries can push past it. `load()` now measures the stream once on entry (`fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END)`, then back to `self._offset`; `load()` already requires a seekable `fp`, since both the TIFF plugin and `Exif` do), keeps a running `total_size` of out-of-line values, and, before the `fp.seek(offset)` / `_safe_read()` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:926-927`, warns `"Tag data larger than file. Skipping tag …"` and `continue`s for any entry that would take the total past the file size, in the same warn-and-skip idiom as the existing "Tag offset too large" check. No fixed constant is introduced and no valid file changes behaviour, including TIFFs with very large Photoshop/ImageSourceData (tag 37724) payloads, which routinely exceed 64 MB. Because `Image.Exif`, the PNG/JPEG/WebP EXIF paths and MPO all go through this one method, they are covered too. The patch adds `test_tag_data_larger_than_file` to `Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py`, next to `test_tag_offset`. With it applied, both paths in the reproducer drop to 1× the file size. One visible side effect: a single oversize entry now skips that tag with this warning instead of aborting the rest of the IFD via the `OSError` path. A fixed module-level cap in the style of `PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_MEMORY` (e.g. a 64 MiB `TiffImagePlugin.MAX_IFD_DATA`) would be the weaker alternative on its own: a 140 KB file could still retain ~63 MiB per IFD — and a JPEG's EXIF is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop), so a 66 KB APP1 segment could still request roughly 1000× its size — and legitimate TIFFs with more than 64 MiB of tag data would lose those tags with a warning. It could still be added on top of the stream-length check as a user-adjustable knob. An alternative that removes the amplification entirely is to store `(offset, size)` in `_tagdata` and read lazily in `__getitem__`, which is what the class docstring already describes ("we don't decode tags unless they're asked for"); that is a larger change because `_tagdata` is shared with `ImageFileDirectory_v1` (`from_v2`/`to_v2`) and exposed as the legacy `tagdata` property, and lazy reads would need the file object to still be open when a tag is first accessed. ## The patch Skip IFD entries once the total out-of-line tag data read by ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() would exceed the size of the stream Applies to `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py index 7b35a0196..ccf923128 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py @@ -500,6 +500,21 @@ def test_tag_offset() -> None: ifd.load(f) +def test_tag_data_larger_than_file() -> None: + ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2() + + # Two BYTE tags that both claim the whole 30 byte IFD as their value + tag_count = struct.pack(" None: base_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2() interop_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2(group=40965) diff --git a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py index 42c1cc96c..c9d506933 100644 --- a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py @@ -892,6 +892,9 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): def load(self, fp: IO[bytes]) -> None: self.reset() self._offset = fp.tell() + fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END) + file_size = fp.tell() + fp.seek(self._offset) try: tag_count = ( @@ -899,6 +902,7 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): if self._bigtiff else self._unpack("H", self._ensure_read(fp, 2)) )[0] + total_size = 0 for i in range(tag_count): tag, typ, count, data = ( self._unpack("HHQ8s", self._ensure_read(fp, 20)) @@ -923,6 +927,16 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): if offset >= 2**63: warnings.warn("Tag offset too large") continue + # The values of a well-formed IFD do not overlap, so in + # total they cannot be larger than the file they are read + # from. RSA decryption was vulnerable to Bleichenbacher timing vulnerabilities, which would impact people using RSA decryption in online scenarios. This is fixed in cryptography 3.2.

Previously, `Cipher.update_into` would accept Python objects which implement the buffer protocol, but provide only immutable buffers:  ```pycon >>> outbuf = b"\x00" * 32 >>> c = ciphers.Cipher(AES(b"\x00" * 32), modes.ECB()).encryptor() >>> c.update_into(b"\x00" * 16, outbuf) 16 >>> outbuf b'\xdc\x95\xc0x\xa2@\x89\x89\xadH\xa2\x14\x92\x84 \x87\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00' ```  This would allow immutable objects (such as `bytes`) to be mutated, thus violating fundamental rules of Python. This is a soundness bug -- it allows programmers to misuse an API, it cannot be exploited by attacker controlled data alone.  This now correctly raises an exception.  This issue has been present since `update_into` was originally introduced in cryptography 1.8.

Issue summary: Processing a maliciously formatted PKCS12 file may lead OpenSSL to crash leading to a potential Denial of Service attack  Impact summary: Applications loading files in the PKCS12 format from untrusted sources might terminate abruptly.  A file in PKCS12 format can contain certificates and keys and may come from an untrusted source. The PKCS12 specification allows certain fields to be NULL, but OpenSSL does not correctly check for this case. This can lead to a NULL pointer dereference that results in OpenSSL crashing. If an application processes PKCS12 files from an untrusted source using the OpenSSL APIs then that application will be vulnerable to this issue.  OpenSSL APIs that are vulnerable to this are: PKCS12_parse(), PKCS12_unpack_p7data(), PKCS12_unpack_p7encdata(), PKCS12_unpack_authsafes() and PKCS12_newpass().  We have also fixed a similar issue in SMIME_write_PKCS7(). However since this function is related to writing data we do not consider it security significant.  The FIPS modules in 3.2, 3.1 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue.

## Vulnerability Summary  The `public_key_from_numbers` (or `EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key()`), `EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key()`, `load_der_public_key()` and `load_pem_public_key()` functions do not verify that the point belongs to the expected prime-order subgroup of the curve.  This missing validation allows an attacker to provide a public key point `P` from a small-order subgroup.  This can lead to security issues in various situations, such as the most commonly used signature verification (ECDSA) and shared key negotiation (ECDH). When the victim computes the shared secret as `S = [victim_private_key]P` via ECDH,  this leaks information about `victim_private_key mod (small_subgroup_order)`. cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. In affected versions `Cipher.update_into` would accept Python objects which implement the buffer protocol, but provide only immutable buffers. This would allow immutable objects (such as `bytes`) to be mutated, thus violating fundamental rules of Python and resulting in corrupted output. This now correctly raises an exception. This issue has been present since `update_into` was originally introduced in cryptography 1.8.

## Summary  In versions of cryptography prior to 46.0.5, DNS name constraints were only validated against SANs within child certificates, and not the "peer name" presented during each validation. Consequently, cryptography would allow a peer named `bar.example.com` to validate against a wildcard leaf certificate for `*.example.com`, even if the leaf's parent certificate (or upwards) contained an excluded subtree constraint for `bar.example.com`.  This behavior resulted from a gap between RFC 5280 (which defines Name Constraint semantics) and RFC 9525 (which defines service identity semantics): put together, neither states definitively whether Name Constraints should be applied to peer names. To close this gap, cryptography now conservatively rejects any validation where the peer name would be rejected by a name constraint if it were a SAN instead.  In practice, exploitation of this bypass requires an uncommon X.509 topology, one that the Web PKI avoids because it exhibits these kinds of problems. Consequently, we consider this a medium-to-low impact severity.  See CVE-2025-61727 for a similar bypass in Go's `crypto/x509`.  ## Remediation  Users should upgrade to 46.0.6 or newer.   ## Attribution  Reporter: @1seal

Issue summary: Processing a maliciously formatted PKCS12 file may lead OpenSSL to crash leading to a potential Denial of Service attack  Impact summary: Applications loading files in the PKCS12 format from untrusted sources might terminate abruptly.  A file in PKCS12 format can contain certificates and keys and may come from an untrusted source. The PKCS12 specification allows certain fields to be NULL, but OpenSSL does not correctly check for this case. This can lead to a NULL pointer dereference that results in OpenSSL crashing. If an application processes PKCS12 files from an untrusted source using the OpenSSL APIs then that application will be vulnerable to this issue.  OpenSSL APIs that are vulnerable to this are: PKCS12_parse(), PKCS12_unpack_p7data(), PKCS12_unpack_p7encdata(), PKCS12_unpack_authsafes() and PKCS12_newpass().  We have also fixed a similar issue in SMIME_write_PKCS7(). However since this function is related to writing data we do not consider it security significant.  The FIPS modules in 3.2, 3.1 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue.

cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. Prior to 46.0.5, the public_key_from_numbers (or EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key()), EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key(), load_der_public_key() and load_pem_public_key() functions do not verify that the point belongs to the expected prime-order subgroup of the curve. This missing validation allows an attacker to provide a public key point P from a small-order subgroup. This can lead to security issues in various situations, such as the most commonly used signature verification (ECDSA) and shared key negotiation (ECDH). When the victim computes the shared secret as S = [victim_private_key]P via ECDH, this leaks information about victim_private_key mod (small_subgroup_order). For curves with cofactor > 1, this reveals the least significant bits of the private key. When these weak public keys are used in ECDSA , it's easy to forge signatures on the small subgroup. Only SECT curves are impacted by this. This vulnerability is fixed in 46.0.5.

Although the limitation that the chain depth cannot exceed a specified maximum depth prevents unbounded recursion and guarantees termination, an attacker-controlled certificate chain can lead the processing to easily take more than 5s to reject in testing. This amplification could form the basis for a resource exhaustion denial of service attack. Gunicorn fails to properly validate Transfer-Encoding headers, leading to HTTP Request Smuggling (HRS) vulnerabilities. By crafting requests with conflicting Transfer-Encoding headers, attackers can bypass security restrictions and access restricted endpoints. This issue is due to Gunicorn's handling of Transfer-Encoding headers, where it incorrectly processes requests with multiple, conflicting Transfer-Encoding headers, treating them as chunked regardless of the final encoding specified. This vulnerability has been shown to allow access to endpoints restricted by gunicorn. This issue has been addressed in version 22.0.0.  To be affected users must have a network path which does not filter out invalid requests. These users are advised to block access to restricted endpoints via a firewall or other mechanism if they are unable to update.

Gunicorn version 21.2.0 does not properly validate the value of the 'Transfer-Encoding' header as specified in the RFC standards, which leads to the default fallback method of 'Content-Length,' making it vulnerable to TE.CL request smuggling. This vulnerability can lead to cache poisoning, data exposure, session manipulation, SSRF, XSS, DoS, data integrity compromise, security bypass, information leakage, and business logic abuse.

Gunicorn fails to properly validate Transfer-Encoding headers, leading to HTTP Request Smuggling (HRS) vulnerabilities. By crafting requests with conflicting Transfer-Encoding headers, attackers can bypass security restrictions and access restricted endpoints. This issue is due to Gunicorn's handling of Transfer-Encoding headers, where it incorrectly processes requests with multiple, conflicting Transfer-Encoding headers, treating them as chunked regardless of the final encoding specified. This vulnerability has been shown to allow access to endpoints restricted by gunicorn. This issue has been addressed in version 22.0.0.  To be affected users must have a network path which does not filter out invalid requests. These users are advised to block access to restricted endpoints via a firewall or other mechanism if they are unable to update.
